findings.content: Regulator would view incomplete security questionnaire as prima facie non-compliance; no mitigating evidence presented.
Auditor would require SOC 2 or equivalent; absence is a material control deficiency regardless of business metrics.
Acquirer technical due diligence would flag missing architecture docs as deal risk; cannot assess scalability or maintainability.
Insurer would require current pen test for cyber policy; absence increases liability exposure post-acquisition.
From customer perspective: revenue growth (E1) irrelevant if service fails due to security gaps (E3); concentration (E2) increases switching cost if vendor fails.
Policy does not define 'current' for pen test; regulator would expect <12 months. Gap in policy precision.
Revenue growth has no bearing on completion of security or technical due-diligence controls.
Customer concentration has no bearing on completion of security or technical due-diligence controls.
An incomplete questionnaire and missing SOC 2 report contradict completion of the required controls, and no external reviewer would accept otherwise.
Revenue growth is favorable context for a customer but does not resolve the security-driven risk profile.
Concentration increases a customer's switching cost, weakening an acceptable-risk-profile claim.
An unresolved security gap contradicts a claim of acceptable risk from every external stakeholder's perspective.

summary: External stakeholder lenses (regulator, auditor, acquirer, insurer, customer) uniformly treat missing security evidence as material risks. Business metrics (E1, E2) do not mitigate technical assurance gaps.
uncertainties: Regulatory jurisdiction and applicable standards not specified
Customer contract terms (SLAs, penalties) not in evidence
